extracted.subtask_description: A news/feature article recounting the Will Smith–Chris Rock incident at the 2022 Oscars, the immediate reactions, subsequent apologies/resignations, and industry responses. Focus is on the aftermath and public commentary rather than legal analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid punching down / joking about medical conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: "Punching down at someone's auto-immune disease is wrong. Doing so on purpose is cruel." (Sophia Bush)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article treats jokes about Jada Pinkett Smith's alopecia as crossing a line; guidance embedded in commentary is that comedians should avoid attacking vulnerable personal conditions—especially on a global stage where the target has publicly shared their struggle.

rubrics_metrics.name: There is no place for violence; assault is unacceptable
rubrics_metrics.description: The Academy "doesn't condone violence" and Will Smith wrote, "There is no place for violence in a world of love and kindness."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple voices in the piece emphasize that physical assault onstage is unacceptable. The expectation is for public figures to condemn violence and for institutions to state that violence will not be tolerated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutions/productions should be prepared with a crisis response
rubrics_metrics.description: Headline/action: "Academy Adds Oscars 'Crisis Team' After Will Smith Slap"; CEO said a crisis team would be at the ready this year, JIC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Award shows and live productions should have protocols and teams in place to manage unexpected onstage incidents, care for affected parties, and manage public messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public apology and acceptance of accountability are expected responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Will Smith apologized publicly and later resigned from the Academy; he wrote he was "out of line and... wrong."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Norms shown in the article: when a celebrity commits a public wrong, the expected remedial steps include issuing a sincere apology, acknowledging wrongdoing, and accepting institutional consequences (resignation, discipline).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedic intent does not excuse harmful impact; context and prior disclosures matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Several voices note that edgy jokes are part of a comedian's act (e.g., "Jokes are what Chris Rock does"), while others stress the particular sensitivity because of Jada's public sharing about an "entanglement" and alopecia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance implied: comedians may rely on edgy material, but should weigh intent against impact—especially when targets have publicly disclosed vulnerability. Awareness of context can prevent punching down or causing undue harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences for onstage assault can include bans, membership stripping, or legal action
rubrics_metrics.description: Reactions included calls that Smith be banned from the Oscars for years or have Academy membership stripped; Jim Carrey said he'd consider suing for $200 million.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece indicates that industry and legal consequences are plausible responses to onstage violence: organizations may impose bans/discipline and affected parties might consider legal remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live productions often continue despite incidents—but this choice draws scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Less than a half hour after the slap, Smith was back onstage accepting his Best Actor Oscar and the show continued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article implies a production tradeoff: continuing the televised event maintains the program flow but can be criticized for normalizing or minimizing the incident; producers must balance show continuity with ethical response and care for those harmed.
